slides.title: In-PE KV Reuse
slides.subtitle: Measured benefits, execution constraints, and an on-wafer secondary KV tier.
slides.notes: Discussion deck: focus on the serving behavior, measured effects, and architecture questions rather than host implementation details.

slides.eyebrow: What has been enabled · serving example
slides.title: A later request can reuse KV left by an earlier request
slides.caption: One slot across three time steps: match the resident prefix, force only the new suffix, then continue normal decode and commit the new resident history.
slides.notes: The example is content-prefix reuse: Request B may have a new sequence ID. Green is already resident, violet is forced input, blue is normal free decode.

slides.title: Resident KV is now a serving resource, not a one-request scratchpad

left.heading: Reuse, rebuild, or replace
left.body: The host chooses a one-to-one resident slot assignment for the batch. The appliance starts from a shared safe prefix, receives no host KV payload on this path, and extends the slot with real prompt and sampled tokens.

highlights: Hit — reuse in place; exact retains one seed, prefix forces only prompt[start:]
Miss — start at zero and rebuild the prompt by force-decode
Pressure — use an empty slot, otherwise replace one whole slot by LRU
slides.notes: Success-only state update matters operationally, but keep the slide at the serving-contract level. Equal-length lanes and one common start are still required.

slides.title: More reusable prefix translates into less round work
slides.caption: Full Qwen3-1.7B, real WSE-3, three repetitions per point. bsz 3–4 reached the PE-memory compile boundary (no TSC); partial shortens the suffix, while exact holds F=1.
slides.notes: At bsz=1 partial R=768 is 1.57× faster than miss; exact R=256 is 1.82×. At bsz=2 the corresponding gains are 1.54× and 1.75×. Most relative SDs are below 0.1%.

slides.title: More slots help only when they cross the working-set threshold
slides.caption: Ten-round synthetic traces, fresh sequence IDs, 256-token shared prefixes. W3 thrashes with two slots but produces seven content hits with four slots: 1.69× lower TSC than no reuse.
slides.notes: W2 is the same with two and four slots; W5 remains no-reuse with both. This isolates temporal locality from exact-ID ownership and from a real workload distribution.

slides.title: Matching works; divergent execution is still missing.
slides.subtitle: Today every lane in a round is forced onto one common safe start, even when its reusable prefix is longer.
slides.notes: This is why the current implementation is still a toy serving setting despite using the full model for the microbenchmarks.

slides.title: One shared start is unfair to requests with long reusable prefixes
slides.caption: Example: Lane A can reuse 768 tokens and Lane B only 256. The current batch starts both at 256; ragged execution would let the same PE block compute different token positions per lane.
slides.notes: This resembles the kernel contract required by continuous batching: per-lane cursor, active mask, forced length and completion state. It may materially change the gain for long system prompts.

slides.title: Seed and decode KV can produce different local reuse depths
slides.caption: After a contiguous host seed and round-robin decode appends, one logical prefix can end at different local indices across PE rows. The current safe mitigation truncates to a shared boundary.
slides.notes: The mitigation loses less than one P-token block. Because the block edge is moderate, this is lower priority than ragged execution. A full solution may require per-row cursors and more on-chip addressing/control.

slides.title: Support flexible placement through measured, static movement profiles
slides.caption: Logical placement can be general, but WSE routes are not keyed by request ID. Each usable storage region should expose capacity plus measured park/reload curves for a precompiled route family.
slides.notes: The planner remains placement-agnostic. The fabric mechanism must still be static/count-exact or serialized through a known mux; arbitrary runtime destinations are not directly supported.

slides.title: A horizontal storage strip gives a simple first mechanism—and a clear capacity bill
slides.caption: Nominal analytical sizing: 42 KiB payload per storage PE and 128 KiB/token across the eight-block model. One 1×256 strip stores about 672 tokens per block; an 8K request needs about 13 rows.
slides.notes: This placement can use vertical gather/scatter and avoid the serpentine inter-block direction at the conceptual level, but color/queue coexistence must be audited. The 42 KiB payload is not yet compile-probed for this storage kernel.

slides.eyebrow: M3 cost model · real CS-3 anchors + analytical candidate
slides.title: At full CS-3 scale, measured host reload crosses recompute
slides.caption: Real Qwen3-1.7B, one WSE-3, Pw512×Ph1024, 2×4 blocks, bsz 1. This E10 resume-only slice crosses near 700 tokens; the green edge-strip band remains analytical.
slides.notes: This is one measured boundary slice, not a universal policy threshold. Full-target reload shifts with S, H and L_new; a true eviction decision must also add decode-to-host D2H and resume probability. E1 must measure the green band.

slides.title: What should we resolve next?

items.action: Prioritize per-lane starts; choose the long-prefix success workload.
Measure bounded reuse loss before moving per-row addressing on-chip.
Sweep park/reload by payload, distance, active rows and direction.
Prototype one profiled edge strip; let measured cost drive eviction.

slides.notes: No decision is implied on arbitrary distributed storage versus a fixed strip. The immediate ask is whether the profile abstraction and edge-strip first probe are the right decomposition.
